newsitem.title: USA: Kasparov vs computer chess battle to resume.
newsitem.headline: Kasparov vs computer chess battle to resume.

text.p: World chess champion Garry Kasparov resumes his battle with the chess-playing supercomputer Deep Blue Tuesday after a day's reflection about how he lost the second game of the 6-game re-match.
Kasparov, considered by most experts to be the best player in chess history, won the first game Saturday with the white pieces but stumbled to defeat in Sunday's game while playing with black.

"We have spent a lot of time looking at Sunday's game, trying to find out why the computer played so well and yet so poorly in the first game," said Frederic Friedel, the champion's closest advisor on computer chess. "Garry learned a lot from studying this game."

The third game of the match starts at 3 p.m. EDT (1900 GMT) Tuesday when Kasparov will again have the slight advantage of the white pieces and the first move, which is similar to having serve in tennis.

The contest, worth $700,000 to the winner and $400,000 to the loser, is a re-match between the 34-year-old Russian grandmaster and the IBM system. Kasparov won the first clash in Philadelphia in February 1996 with three wins, two draws and a loss over six games.
The system, which can calculate hundreds of millions of positions per second, is faster than it was last year and has been programmed with more chess knowledge.

His game one loss in Philadelphia and Sunday's defeat were the only occasions that a chess-playing computer had defeated a reigning world champion in a classical chess format, in which games can last several hours.

Part chess competition and part research project to help build computers that can make complex, simultaneous calculations at high speeds, the games are being played on the 35th floor of a skyscraper Manhattan office complex.

IBM says that among the applications for the technology developed for Deep Blue are weather forecasting, air traffic control, data mining and molecular dynamics. Deep Blue is an IBM RS/6000 SP parallel processor with specialised microchips for chess.
